utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And ... Your Honour, as I requested yesterday, the time that we requested for this witness was one full session today but we will try and limit that, and I do apologise for this discrepancy between the time that we requested and the time that we actually will use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'd forgotten is to remind Mr. Wilson that he is still bound by his solemn declaration he gave in the beginning of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you may proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, we left off yesterday in mid-sentence, as it were, and it was that proposition that I made. We were discussing the column leaving. That's on line 15, page 4039 of the transcript. We said that that was in March 1992, and my -- I put it to you that that event actually occurred on the 15th of May, and that on this occasion, some 59 members, JNA members, were killed while this column was trying to pull out. Now, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think your date is probably more likely to be correct than mine, but I'm unaware of the exact number of people who were injured or killed in the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But in any case, you do know that there were casualties, both dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, if we know that on the 3rd of May during the evacuation of the command in Sarajevo there was an incident, and that there was an incident while the garrison was trying to pull out of Tuzla, and that there was another incident when the Jusuf Dzonlic barracks was evacuated - that was in Sarajevo - would you then agree with me that General Mladic's concern for the security of these pullouts was quite justified?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing of the detail of the first two barracks evacuations, but on the basis of the Jusuf Dzonlic barracks, the execution of that evacuation, I think General Mladic had reason to be nervous about the success of executing the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, answering the Prosecutor's question on page 3966 about the evacuation of the Jusuf Dzonlic barracks you said that around 30 vehicles were lost on the following day, as well as 30 men. Now, in the days that followed, did you learn anything about the fate of these 30 men?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to the extent that neither side seemed to be particularly concerned about it within about 48 hours of the event, so I assume it was resolved satisfactorily. Neither side asked us to take any action to assist them to resolve the issue. So I assume it was satisfactorily fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could we now have P321, please, on the monitors. We need page 7 in the B/C/S, in the Serbian version, and page 7 as well in the English version. You know this document. It is about the evacuation of the JNA garrison, and it -- from the barracks, and it was compiled on the 20th of May. Now, General, sir, on page 3941 of October 10, you said that in the end it was General Mladic who prevented their pullout from the city, and you were referring to the pullout of some 2.000 people that were supposed to be evacuated by -- through a humanitarian organisation from Sarajevo and taken to the coast. Now, General, sir, if you now take a look at the next page - that's paragraph 8 in English - there it says that Colonel Cadjo, the liaison officer, JNA liaison officer, called to advice that General Mladic had heard that the column with children was not to leave that night. Now, General, sir, my question is this: Did you ever hear from Colonel Cadjo that General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think my friend may have misspoken when he was reading the text, at least as it appears in English. I heard him to say, General Mladic had heard that the children's embassy or convoy is not to leave tonight when it is written that "General Mladic had word."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we all agree on that to be the proper reading then it is hereby corrected. And you may proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I can accept that. But my question was really about something else. So General, sir, did you ever hear from Colonel Cadjo that General Mladic had ordered that this children convoy was not to leave on that night?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the source of the information 20 years after the event, but it was quite clear -- it is quite clear in my recollection that the convoy was not going anywhere without General Mladic's authority and he was tying its release in events to the barracks. He was using the convoy as a bargaining tool. Whether it was Colonel Cadjo or General Mladic who said the convoy wasn't leaving, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the previous page, or, actually, paragraph 5 of this document, you will see there, and let me ask if you will agree with me, that after the agreement was reached the Presidency called and came up with a new proposition, proposal, that the JNA did not accept; in other words, was it the Presidency that changed the agreement that had previously been agreed around this convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may well have been. There was constant bargaining going backwards and forwards. I'm simply in this cable stating what the bargaining position was at a point in time. At some point after this cable the children were -- were -- the convoy was released. Barracks was delivered to the food [sic] and both sides were happy. Counsel, this is just a record of bargaining positions at -- at a point in time before it is finally resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 65 ter 27602.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is an intercept dated the 24th of May, 1992, and in the middle of page 1 you can see that one of the participants in this conversation was Milosav Gagovic, and he says there that the Viktor Bubanj barracks had been evacuated and that they had left alive healthy and there was not a bullet was fired? Now, on the following page - in English that will be page 3, line 2, starting with RM, the initials RM. And in the original -- in the original transcript, it says Ratko Mladic. And then we can read the following: "Pass on the message to your men to keep the situation calm. Do not allow any shooting anymore, otherwise you will spoil things for me. Inform all your people that Viktor Bubanj barracks has been relocated with no casualties or fire." General, sir, now when you see this intercept, can you tell us what it is in your view that General Mladic is referring to when he says "do not allow any shooting anymore, otherwise you'll spoil things for me"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation is that he is seeking to impose a cease-fire in that area and he doesn't want his soldiers in that area firing or it may disrupt future evacuations of the barracks. And he demonstrates, if not on this occasion but certainly on other occasions, that when he wants to he can impose a cease-fire on the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's continue with this intercept. Let's see now page -- the following -- the next page in English where Ratko Mladic says: "And we should not burn and destroy all around us. Let's give peace a chance." General, sir, when it says "burn and destroy," does that imply the use of some artillery weapon?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It includes, in my view, all types of firing. He is trying to calm down one of his commanders. He's trying to make sure the situation is quiet so he is unlikely to be using wild or provocative language. He is trying to calm people down here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm still not seeing the portion of the intercept that was being referred to about burning everything down. I'm not sure what page this is on in English. Oh -- I think -- I see the line. I think it's just perhaps not -- the translation -- is my friend referring to where he says, "and we shall not destroy everything around us"? That is what is written in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely it. It is probably to do with the translation or interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence will propose, will move to tender this document, with -- to MFI it, in view of the Defence's position regarding our -- the final decision about intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand this. You ask questions and you ask, How do you understand this, Mr. Mladic said this, How did you interpret that? And at the same time you're reserving the right to challenge the authenticity of it. How would we understand the testimony of this witness if you say, Well, but we say it's not Mr. Mladic but please tell us what Mr. Mladic said or how we have to understand that. Isn't that a bit inconsistent, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can agree with you. However, if the Trial Chamber adopts the view that those documents are authentic, I did not want to miss this opportunity to question this witness about what he knew about this intercept, or related to this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic, it is not only what the Chamber will say about it. It -- the issue is what your position is. You are asking the witness questions about it. Apparently you do not want to tender it. You said you want it to be MFI'd. We'll consider it during the break, but, of course, the Chamber would like -- if you use the document, that you take a clear position.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I just be heard briefly on that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I agree with the observation that Your Honour made that you can't basically have your cake and eat it too. Either this is General Mladic speaking and your acknowledging General Mladic is speaking and therefore you're asking for comments on what he said, or else there's no relevance to the questions that are posed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, of course, there is another matter; that is, that if this witness would be have been called, well, let's say, in half a year for now and if matters on authenticity would have been settled then, of course, the dilemma would not exist any further for the Defence. So I'd like -- I prefer to have it MFI'd at this moment, not necessarily for the reason Mr. Petrusic gave but for the Chamber to consider whether we accept or not this way of proceeding. Madam Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 27602 will be D75, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. You may proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, finally, did you know that there were military targets in Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Pofalici is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are through with our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Any need to re-examine the witness, Ms. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could have D75 MFI back on the screen, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General Wilson, do you have -- have you ever heard of Obrad Popadic before seeing this intercept today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Any idea who that individual was or what role he may have played in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you know if he a member of the JNA or the VRS or some other armed force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this individual at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I take it you had no knowledge of this conversation before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen this intercept in the last few days, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So no personal knowledge of it prior to that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And so the answers given to counsel today, are they based on any knowledge or just your best guesses or speculation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation. Best guesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could -- if I could refresh your memory as to some conversation you had with counsel yesterday. One of the areas that were asked questions about was the media. And this appears at page, for my friend's assistance, 4007 to 4008 of the transcript when my friend put to you this question: "General, sir, can you agree with me that there were a lot of sources in the media, a lot of information leaked -- was leaked through the media to shape the public opinion, and the sources for that information was rather unreliable, or rather, they were biased." And you responded: "Information, manipulation of information is one of the weapons of war. Both during the war in Bosnia and virtually every other conflict. The accuracy of media reports is often questionable and needs to be verified by reliable means before accepting it as fact, and this is what we attempted to do." General Wilson, are you saying that there were -- every media report from every agency during the Bosnian war was incorrect, or would you need to look at the individual articles or reports to comment on their accuracy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton is that not perfectly clear from the answer. The question was phrased in a way which, of course, would lead to no successful -- I mean, would lead to nothing which would assist the Chamber. Generally to say that leaked information would not be reliable, of course, the witness then perfectly said is that: What you need to do is to check on every single occasion, whether it's reliable or not by verifying it. And he certainly did not even hint at what you now present as a possible way of understanding his answer. I think his answer was so clear that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My last area, sir, is with respect to some questions you were asked about a special incident report from the 30th of May, 1992, which was P336. That was a report about firing on UNPROFOR vehicles on the 30th of May, 1992, when you were going to Lukavica barracks to meet with General Mladic. Do you recall that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could we have P332 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that -- Mr. Wilson, when I would have understood -- when I would have misunderstood your answer I just said was so obvious, I take it that you would have immediately intervened and said, No, you have totally misunderstood my answer. But I thought it was very clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You see before you, sir, that this is the document we've discussed earlier. The record of your meeting on the 30th of May, 1992, with General Mladic. And I wonder if we could please turn to page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S, and we're going to look at paragraph 8. So in answer to questions yesterday asked by my friend, you gave the following response to the question: "Was fire ever opened at you or at the UNPROFOR vehicles by the members of the VRS that controlled that road?" And you said: "We were fired on many occasions along that route, including one occasion my vehicle was hit or two vehicles we were travelling in, convoy. We were hit 32 times and lost six of the eight tires in our vehicle. Inevitably, when we raised this with the two parties they would say it was the other party or we have no control of that area. We never successfully identified who was responsible for these attacks." Paragraph 8 of the document in front of you indicates: "General Mladic apologised for the firing on UN vehicles passing Marsal Tito barracks (special incident reports refers) and blames this on the fact that the people in the barracks had become irresponsible because of the firing they had been subjected to recently?" With respect to that occasion, were you able to get an admission from one of the parties as to who had been responsible for the firing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's outlined in paragraph 8 there. General Mladic accepts the responsibility that it was some irresponsible individual from the JNA. And in regard to your question yesterday, I -- I thought the question was had I been fired upon on my journey of that day from the PTT to the meeting with General Mladic, and I said I couldn't recall about whether I was fired upon for that particular journey. I think we are -- if I misinterpreted your question yesterday, then so be it. But perhaps right now we're talking about two different incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. I think I have confused you. Perhaps we need to look at the special incident report, which is P336.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, I've got the wrong exhibit number. Sorry, it's P -- P341, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So this is an incident that occurred on the 30th of May, 1992, when you were travelling to Lukavica, not the incident we discussed previously of the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that I've seen this report and I've refreshed my memory, yes, we were fired upon on that journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions in re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bolton. The Chamber has no further questions for you either. Mr. Petrusic, have the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Wilson, this then concludes your testimony before this Court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the -- either by the parties or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considered how we would proceed. We have a few procedural matters, not much. It's about the pace of filing of 92 bis. It may also be an oral decision on a motion. And the Defence motion to -- in large, time to respond to the sixth 92 bis motion. These are relatively minor matters. The Chamber would like to know whether the parties have anything they would like to raise. Not to do it now, just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two very brief matters which I think could be appropriately raised in Mr. Mladic's absence. It's just willing to provide information to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly why I am taking at this moment an inventory of what we have to do, so that Mr. Mladic, who I do understand is present on the premises, knows if he decides that he wants to return to court which he is free to do that he knows at least what the subject matter will be after the break, so if you could just indicate what approximately it is you would raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's just to provide information with respect to two exhibits that we undertook to provide the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then has the Defence any matter it would like to raise this morning? Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a short break, that is a break of 15 minutes. Therefore, we'll resume at 10.25. And, as matters stand now, it is very likely that we would conclude this hearing at quarter to 11.00, approximately. My guess would be that we would need some 20 minutes. We resume at 25 minutes past 10.00. --- Break taken at 10.10 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I establish the presence of the accused in the courtroom. Then we had a few procedural matters. The first one, Mr. Groome, was about the pace of filing of 92 bis and quater motions as they are completed and then to develop the schedule for the Defence when to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The previous guidance of the Chamber was always two to three weeks apart, but that was the previous guiding. The Chamber grants your request. You may file the 92 bis and quater motions once they are ready. And I think the Defence's position was you would ask for further time, and I think we have received a first request for further time and we will look at that, of course. With -- we'll most likely grant that so you have always reasonable time, if you are flooded with 92 bis motions that you had adequate time to respond. We have received the first request and we'll decide on that soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it would assist the Defence and the Chamber and the Prosecution of all -- of being aware of the status of these, the Prosecution would be happy to undertake including a table that would have all of the pending 92 bis issues at the end of the witness schedule that we have been producing every few weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be appreciated. Second, there was a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just give us one second to find something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber would like to deliver a decision, a decision on the Prosecution's motion to amend its 65 ter witness list by substituting Fatima Pita for Witness RM154, Ekrem Pita, a motion which was filed on 7th of September, 2012. The Defence has filed a response on the 21st of September, indicating that it does not oppose the motion. The Chamber grants the motion. The Prosecution may amend its 65 ter witness list by substituting Ekrem Pita by Fatima Pita. The Chamber has considered both that the new witness was an eye-witness to the event, whereas, the old witness was not. It is in the interest of justice to grant the motion. Also, the Chamber has considered that the Defence did not oppose the motion. And that concludes the decision of the Chamber on this matter. Then the third matter I had on my list is that the Defence asked to enlarge the time the Defence will have to respond to the Prosecution's sixth motion to admit evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. This was filed on the 11th of October, and the request was 14 more days to respond to that sixth motion. Since the deadline for the response is today then the Chamber wonders whether there's any objection to the motion being granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution. Then the Chamber grants this motion, and the Defence has 14 additional days to respond to it. These were the matters the Chamber had on its list. Is there any -- Mr. Groome, you had two brief matters, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first one related to D55, and Your Honours may recall this was a map of the Kozarac and Omarska area, and Your Honour had raised the -- questions about the -- the projection angle of the document, and I undertook to investigate that matter. We have spoken to our mapping unit, and they inform us that it -- the scale at the bottom would not be a reliable way to judge distances, and -- the Chamber should be cautioned against doing so but that the map would be accurate with respect to the relationship of the different locations but certainly not the scale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this was due to the projection angle or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't have that precise information. I will say, Your Honour, that many of these maps are old and at this stage the Prosecution does have far more sophisticated technology with determining distance. So if any distance at any time becomes of importance or is deemed important by the Chamber or even the Defence, the Prosecution is happy to seek to get that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I may add that if you do not make any projection under a certain angle then you don't even need sophisticated technology. You can just look at the map, measure it, and then you have the answer. That's the reason why -- and I'm now speaking for myself for the last ten year I've always insisted on having non-projected maps but maps that someone can use. Perhaps for the future. Then the second matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second matter, Your Honour, relates to D59. And, if you will recall, this was a document that had some handwritten text on the original document that had not been translated. And the Prosecution undertook to see if it could locate another copy that did not have such handwriting. We were able to query our collection and found another copy of this document without a handwritten note. We have sent that to the Defence this morning. And Ms. Janet Stewart informs me that there is different handwriting on this note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we -- I maybe spoke too early on this issue. We have sent a copy of what we have discovered in our collection to the Defence this morning, and we'll discuss it further which is the most appropriate copy to have in evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome, then the Chamber will wait and see what happens in relation to D59. Mr. Stojanovic, there was nothing else to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had an opportunity to see this today, and we will wait for the official version to come our way. We've only had opportunity to see it here in the courtroom, and then we will respond to that, to that part which was handwritten and which is clear to me because it is in the language I speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if the parties would reach any agreement which would be the most appropriate -- which would be the most appropriate copy to be used, then the Chamber would prefer to receive a shared position of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no doubt that that will be the case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if there's nothing else we adjourn. But. Mr. Stojanovic, it's only a couple of days ago that the Chamber inquired in some detail on how much time the cross-examination of the present witness would take so as to be able to see whether we could still use any time remaining this Friday. The indication was then still six hours. Later it became four hours. And it turns out now out to be even far less than that. Would you, please, if we ask this kind of information be very precise in your analysis on how much time you would need, because time claimed and not used is, under the present circumstances, time lost, and we would try to avoid that. If there's no other matter, we have two non-sitting weeks, which means that we adjourn for the day, and will resume on Monday, the 29th of October, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
